# **Public Engagement — OR Briefing Book** 

## Why “public engagement”? 

*Note: This section describes how engagement works today, and broadly what is meant to achieve. It does not define what "good" engagement means; **that is left to delegates.***

About 266,000 people live in Crook, Deschutes, and Jefferson counties, and nearly every part of their daily lives is shaped by state and local government. (Census, July 2025 estimates) This includes decisions about how our land and natural resources are managed, what kind of businesses are allowed to be here and where (zoning), how our schools are managed, how public health is protected, and much more. Each of these is managed by one or more departments at the city, county, and state levels (or sometimes, federal, in the case of certain public lands). 

People who live in Oregon have the right and the opportunity to provide input into the decisions that affect them.  We affect some of those decisions through electing representatives, but we also have other means to weigh in on specific decisions.

**Effective public engagement helps ensure that public sector decisions are informed not only by technical expertise, but also by the knowledge, values, priorities, and personal experiences of the people who will be affected by those decisions and whose tax dollars support them.** 

Examples of formal public engagement in state and local decisions include:

* **State legislative hearings,** and city council and county commission meetings that are open to the public and invite public comment  
* **Town halls** on specific topics  
* **Surveys**  
* **Public comment periods** when local or state rules are being drafted  
* **Public meetings** organized by local or state elected officials  
* **Public Hearings required by state and local law in the matters of local legislation and quasi-judicial land use applications (i.e. code updates, conditional use permits, zone changes, etc.)**  
* **Initiatives and referenda,** through which citizens and advocacy groups can place items on the ballot for the public to approve or deny  
* **Boards and commissions,** where citizens may be appointed.   
* And, of course, **elections.**

## Who gets involved in public decisions?

Our state and local governments may be responsible for making the final decisions, but many groups take part in public decisions. Each plays a different role. 

| Who | What they do | Central Oregon examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Government** | Makes and carries out decisions. State decisions often set the rules that local governments must follow. | State agencies, county commissions, city councils, school boards, special districts, public advisory commissions made up of members of the public |
| **Individuals** | Every resident has the right to take part in local decisions, both through formal means (public meetings, comment periods, public hearings, etc) and informal means (organizing petitions, direct actions, etc).  | Speaking at a council meeting, emailing a commissioner, etc. |
| **Organized residents** | When residents organize, officials tend to see them as speaking for a broader group, not just one person.  |  |
| **Advocacy groups** | Speak for a cause or community. They often follow issues closely and comment on behalf of members, or file lawsuits. | Central Oregon LandWatch, The Environmental Center, 1000 Friends of Oregon, Oregon Rural Action, Bend Privacy Alliance, etc. |
| **Businesses and business groups** | Often have significant sway. They may sell services to government, seek incentives to locate here, or hire lobbyists to advocate on their behalf. | Local businesses, AI companies, real estate developers or agents |
| **Public-Private Coordinators** | Separate organizations that develop strategies for the development of the region and coordinate across the public and private spheres. Organizations like EDCO may also be involved in recruiting, keeping, and supporting businesses that move to the region.  | Economic Development for Central Oregon, Central Oregon Intergovernmental Council |

**Public Private Negotiations**

Many government decisions related to AI in particular involve companies that are selling services to the government (e.g., MagicSchoolAI selling its software to local school districts), or working with the government to develop their operations in the area (e.g., data center developments). Compared to decisions that go through local councils or planning commissions, these are often less visible to the public. 

**On the other hand, there could also be good reasons for these private dealings to remain private.** The Economic Development Corporation of Central Oregon (EDCO) says early recruitment is often kept confidential to protect companies' competitive information and workers. It calls these confidentiality agreements a real limit, not bad faith, though it often means the public learns of a project after major terms are set. To them, they believe that the appropriate places for public input comes through elected officials, its three-year community strategy meetings, and public votes on long-term incentives.

## How and when can the public get involved?

Engagement can happen before the government makes a decision, while it is being made, and after it takes effect. At each stage, there are important opportunities for residents, corporations, and others outside the government to shape the decisions to meet their interests.

| Stage | Why | Common examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Before (Notice, Education)**  | Opportunities to learn about the issue and its impacts, so that later engagement is well-informed and impactful | Public notices, mailing lists, staff reports, explainers, educational sessions, City and County email listservs, etc.  |
| **During (Feedback, Deliberation)**  | Offering feedback on what the proposed decisions do well and poorly, so that they can be improved before they are implemented.  | Public comment during council meetings, advisory committees, budget hearings |
| **After (Accountability, Appeals)**  | Checking in to make sure that the implemented policy is doing what it was intended to do, with reasonable resources | Regular reporting on results, audits, appeals, oversight bodies, lawsuits, etc |

**The Floor: What is the minimum public engagement that the government has to support, and what *could* they support?**

There are three main ways that the public is currently *mandated* to participate via state and local laws: **public notices** ahead of meetings, **comments** during public meetings, and various **boards and commissions** that members of the public can serve on. This is what we call the “floor” of public engagement, but public agencies and officials can always choose to do more. 

| Opportunity | Stage  | What the law requires |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Notices** | Before | Advance notice is required for public meetings (at least 48 hours for regular and 24 hours for special meetings). Mailed notices are required for property owners near land use decisions, and state agencies must publish notice at least 21 days before adopting rules. *([ORS 197.763](https://www.oregonlaws.org/ors/197.763), [ORS 183.335](https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors183.html))* |
| **Public Comment** | During | Public meetings allowing in-person testimony must also permit remote testimony. Public comment is required at hearings for land use cases, local budget decisions, state rule changes, and utility rate or water right proceedings. Enterprise zone tax agreements over three years require resolutions at public meetings. *([Oregon Public Meetings Law](https://www.oregon.gov/transparency/pages/public-meetings.aspx))* |
| **Boards & Commissions** | During and/or After | These groups of people meet regularly to provide public oversight and decisionmaking over certain aspects of government. For example, via [Oregon’s Local Budget Law](https://www.ci.carlton.or.us/media/9666), local governments require citizen budget committees that are composed of both appointed public members of city/county councilors. Planning commissions operate similarly, where officers review and approve land use proposals (Statewide Planning Goal 1).  At the state level, the Governor appoints members to over 265 state boards and commissions, and electric cooperatives hold member-elected board elections.  |

There are also a few notable places where decisions might leave the eye of the public. These practices are not necessarily  meant to obscure public involvement, but allow the government to execute on its mission efficiently: 

* **Legislative versus executive decisions.** Councils, commissions, and the Legislature set policy in public meetings, where the public is able to more directly engage. However, executive offices and government staff carry out their duties in accordance with those policies, and can make decisions or set priorities with little public review. Public review on every single decision that the government makes would quickly grind public service to a halt; rather than encourage that, most government activity can be investigated through meeting logs, information requests, or otherwise.   
  * In Prineville, community input on enterprise zone agreements came through elected officials (the mayor, city council, and county commissioners), with no separate public process.   
* **By-right zoning.** While many land use decisions will go through a Planning Commission before they are finalized, some uses of land might be approved “outright” or “by-right,” meaning they can bypass this review. This is also in the spirit of efficiency, given that the use case is safe and it already falls in line with a use case that the city/county wants to develop around. This is the case in Prineville, where data centers are allowed outright in the industrial park on the rim of the city and utilities have already been upgraded to support them.   
* **Nondisclosure Agreements (NDAs).** Larger businesses will frequently establish NDAs that keep the details of their negotiations, the business details, etc private unless they intentionally choose to share it. This is usually done because   
  * For data centers in particular, the environment around this might be changing; Amazon recently announced that they will no longer pursue NDAs when engaging with city governments. This would allow the public to get more advanced notice before major developments from the company come to town. 

**The Ceiling: Where could the public have more involvement?** 

![][image1]

**The "ceiling" is how much power the public could have, beyond what the law requires.** Depending on funding and interest, public officials can create more opportunities for meaningful public engagement. 

**Who gets to take part?** Having a chance to engage is not the same as being able to use it. Meetings may happen during working hours, go on for hours, or follow rules that limit what people can say. Barriers in Central Oregon include language and interpretation, disability access, work and caregiving schedules, distance and transportation, internet access, and trust in institutions. These look different across ages: a working parent, a retiree, and a high school student each face different hurdles. Two questions to keep in mind for every stage: who is missing, and who keeps getting asked?

## Before a decision: notice, information, due diligence

### **Advanced Notice**

**People need to hear about decisions that matter to them early enough to contribute.**

**Why it matters:** 

Simply put, you can't weigh in on something you don't know about. When people are left out, the government can make decisions that accidentally harm them, and trust drops, which makes compromise harder later. Local leaders said people are often brought in only after a decision is mostly made. 

\> *“I think it’s important to have the community engagement piece far enough in advance from the organizational standpoint, the decision making standpoint, that decisions aren’t already made. It has to be still in the point where you can adjust strategies and not even really change the plan.”* – Rachel Haakenson, NeighborImpact

\>\> Any firsthand account from La Pine residents about notice and timing on the proposed data center? 

**What it looks like:**

* **Meeting notices.** Oregon's Public Meetings Law requires notice of every meeting of a governing body at least 48 hours ahead for regular meetings and 24 hours for special ones. Notices must list the date, time, place, how to join online, and the main topics. *\[[City of Springfield summary of OGEC training](https://springfield-or.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Memo-Oregon-Public-Meeting-Law_Final.pdf), Dec 2025\]*  
* **Mailing lists.** Many local governments let you sign up to get public notices and agendas by email (e.g., Crook County and the City of Prineville).   
* **Land use notices.** By law, cities and counties must mail notice at least 20 days ahead to nearby property owners for many land use decisions and public hearings: within 100 feet inside an urban growth boundary, 250 feet outside one, and 750 feet in farm or forest zones. Renters and people farther away may not get a letter. *([ORS 197.763](https://www.oregonlaws.org/ors/197.763))*

**Challenges**

‘Neighbor notice’ of specific land use applications is limited to landowners within 500 feet or less of the location where the project is proposed. In practice, in rural areas, this amounts to very few people. 

Additionally, neighbor notices can be difficult to understand because they rely on legal and land use jargon. Existing state and local rules require that notice of certain public hearings be posted in the newspaper, but newspaper circulation is decreasing and few Central Oregonians rely on the classified section of the local paper for their information about local municipal affairs. (Robin Hayakawa, Central Oregon LandWatch). 

### **Information**

**People need accurate, balanced information to take part in a meaningful way.**

**Why it matters:** 

Well-informed people can advocate for what will truly help them and against real harms. This includes learning about the topic itself (for example, the positive and negative impacts of using AI in the classroom), what decision is being made, who makes it, and on what timeline. 

On the other hand, misinformation can be a significant barrier to productive engagement. Multiple public officials in the region noted that they had seen misinformation about the impacts of AI-powered technologies, data centers, etc. influence how people reacted to proposals. While it is not the source of misinformation, local governments and elected officials can counter misinformation by proactively reaching out to residents and ensuring that accurate, transparent data is widely available.

**“Central Oregon has massive disparities in AI literacy. We need to help get everyone up to speed on the risks and opportunities AI poses to our communities.”**

**– Open Poll participant. 67% of participants agreed with them.** 

**“There needs to be more education on AI for the general public before many of these statements can be addressed. …no way to know if what I am reading/seeing is real or AI so I don't trust it anymore.”**

**– Open Poll participant. 85% agreed.** 

**\>\>  Adam Young** pointed to a local claim that Ochoco Reservoir is low because of data centers as a reason for myth-versus-fact resources. 

**What it looks like:** 

* **Accessible, balanced educational materials** that explain the nature of the decisions being made, pros and cons, etc.   
* **Opportunities to sit down with public officials** who are responsible for the decision  
* **Funding local news** and information distributors  
* **Asking specific questions.** Instead of only asking "data center or no data center," Adam Young suggested asking where it would go and what its effects would be on the environment, light, and noise.  
* **Learning from places that have faced similar problems**

**Challenges**

Good information often has to be pulled from many sources, and gathering it can be time intensive. People may not already agree on which details are important, or even what the truth of a matter is.

Depending on the nature of the decision and potential confidentiality issues, there may not be enough time or information for the general public to educate themselves sufficiently on a topic to understand the nuances and the potential pros and cons of an issue. Passionate advocacy based on an incomplete or incorrect understanding of the issues can not only lead to suboptimal decisions but also to a breakdown in trust on both sides of the discussion that can continue to color discussions well into the future. 

It is generally difficult to expect people to dig into heavy, technical issues unless it was their job to understand them. This leaves residents relying on elected and appointed officials*.*  In other places public commissions of everyday residents have taken many months or even years to understand the impacts. 

### **Due diligence**

**Decision-makers need good information from all sides, and they need to weigh the possible effects on the community.**

**Why it matters:** 

Public officials are expected to explain their decisions, justify how public money was used, and report on results. Knowing they will be expected to do so reinforces the importance of careful decision-making and stewardship of public funds, as well as responsiveness to the people they serve.

**What it looks like:** 

Officials often ask for reports, briefings, and expert advice, and staff help produce them and connect officials with experts. This work has two parts: *the facts* (what is actually happening?) and *public preferences* (what do people actually want?). Ideally, this information gathering is transparent to the public, so that residents and advocates can call out potential gaps or draw their own conclusions.

As a relevant example, representatives from the City of Prineville’s planning department say it treats data centers like any large industrial project: study the demand, check whether there is enough capacity, then negotiate development agreements and incentives. This is required by law, as they 

## During a decision: feedback and deliberation

### **Feedback**

**Members of the public get a chance to weigh in on policies before they are final.**

**Why it matters.** Feedback is a chance for members of the public to share why a proposed policy or plan will or will not work for their community. They can offer data, personal experience, professional expertise, preferences, and community needs to hopefully improve plans to need the needs and values of more people. It is also an opportunity for public officials to explain what they are considering and why. 

**What it looks like.** Spaces for public feedback look different for different government bodies. Below are a few examples from different formal and informal public bodies. 

| Who | What they did | What changed |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Bend-La Pine Schools** | Board policy goes through required public comment. Parent and student voice councils also give input. | The classroom chatbot lost its human-like persona and now flags emotional conversations to teachers. Adults now disclose AI use in grading. Teachers may not use AI plagiarism-detection tools on English-learner students. *\[Verify against policy text\]* |
| **NeighborImpact** | For its biennial plan, surveys about problems (not proposed solutions) were distributed to those receiving services, listening sessions in every city plus online and Spanish-language sessions.(Note: NeighborImpact is not a government entity, but they face similar challenges and their experiences can help inform government practices.)  | Decision-makers hear residents directly, and are more likely to prioritize what they heard.  |
| **Cascades East Transit** | Spanish-language survey of Madras residents with the Latino Community Association, under an ODOT grant. | Surveys and fare data led to 15-minute service on Third Street and a planned microtransit pilot in south Bend. |

Intermediary organizations like Neighborimpact, COCAP, Oregon Kitchen Table, etc.  play a role in connecting the community with decisionsmakers. These organizations often have more room to navigate than government because engagement is their primary focus, they have the training, and they do not have to navigate the same rules and priorities that might hamstring government agencies around community engagement. 

**Challenges.**

* **Who is heard.** Good feedback reflects the whole community, not just a few loud voices or tokenized people. But comment processes often favor the most motivated people, professionals, and interested parties with their own goals and the time, capacity, and training to do it effectively. Creating effective spaces for public consultation takes funding and training many departments often don't have, or haven’t allocated towards that purpose.  
* **What to engage them on.** Some decisions are already fixed by law, so asking the public about them is just box-checking. Engagement works best when it focuses on what can actually change.

### **Deliberation**

**The public can be invited to discuss and weigh the tradeoffs of a decision together.**

**Why it matters:** 

Making good decisions around policies requires people to not only gather good information, but to talk through the values they hold and tradeoffs between different options. Inside a government entity, deliberation happens all the time: councils and boards debate before they vote. The public is rarely asked to do this to inform policies, but when this is done well, it can produce decisions that the majority of residents support. When people must decide together, "the incentives are problem-solving incentives rather than \[political\] incentives” (Wendy Willis of Oregon Kitchen Table).

**What it looks like:** 

The various boards and commissions that operate throughout Central Oregon have elements of deliberation, in that they have non-elected citizens discussing public issues together to make decisions. However, these conversations only take place among a small group of people, rather than engaging. When the public is brought in for things like public comment, there is rarely space for two-way conversation between residents or representatives. 

The gold standard of good deliberation is that which is **inclusive, representative, informed, and conversational** – in other words, many different kinds of affected people talking and considering each other’s reasons for what they believe**.** Juries are the most common example of public deliberation in practice, where a randomly selected group of residents learns about an issue and makes recommendations together. But there are many other examples of how this can happen: 

* **Deschutes County** formed a civic assembly on youth homelessness in fall 2025 that identified 22 actionable recommendations (See: [Healthy Democracy case study](https://healthydemocracy.org/home/projects/deschutescivicassembly/))  
* **Oregon's Citizens' Initiative Review** brings together a random panel of voters to study a ballot measure and write a statement for the voters' pamphlet summarizing their support (or lack thereof) and their reasoning.   
* **Mosier, Oregon.** After a train derailment, Oregon's Kitchen Table led a quick community conversation so the town knew what residents wanted before negotiating with the railroad. 

**Challenges:**

* **Doing deliberation well takes a lot of time and money.** Recruitment of a representative group is especially challenging for reasons represented above; the people who are most likely to show up are often those with more privilege in one way or another (socioeconomic status, English-speaking, etc). It can take a lot of time and money to overcome these challenges, which can quickly exhaust both participants and government staff.    
* **Lack of training.** Running a good meeting (one that tries to achieve a balance of voices, navigate conflict, etc) often requires experienced facilitators who can be hard to find and expensive to hire. 

## After a decision: accountability and appeal

### **Accountability**

**The government shares what happened after a policy takes effect, checks that it was a good use of public money, and is ready to change course if needed.** 

**Why it matters.** Accountability means public officials, through open processes, explain their decisions, justify how public money was used, report on results, and take responsibility for how things turned out. At the very least, it means closing the loop with the people who gave input. **Kathi Barguil said institutions often lose people at this step: they ask for ideas, then never say how the input was used or why it wasn't. "Community members want to know that the time that they put in mattered."** 

**What it looks like.**

* **Feedback requirements for technologies.** A public list of state AI uses is expected by mid-2027, along with an annual report to the Governor and an AI adoption plan from each agency. Public-facing AI must have a way for users to give feedback, with review and escalation.   
* **Addressing Concerns.** For example, the Oregon Department of Land Conservation and Development (DLCD) developed an Offshore Wind Energy Roadmap defining standards for offshore wind development. The process involved extensive public review and input from a multi-stakeholder Roundtable assembled in 2024\. In July 2026, DLCD published the final Roadmap alongside a detailed document of DLCD Responses to Public Comments, demonstrating how community feedback was considered and integrated into the final standards.  
* **Audits.** The Oregon Secretary of State's Audits Division reviews how state agencies spend money and whether programs work, and [publishes its findings.](https://sos.oregon.gov/audits/Pages/default.aspx)

### **Appeal**

**If a decision or policy isn't working, or wasn't made properly, the public should have ways to challenge it.**

**Why it matters:** No one can predict exactly how a policy will turn out when it is implemented. Creating opportunities for the public to appeal decisions allows us to structurally improve policies so that potential harms can be avoided. 

**What it looks like.**

* **School decisions.** In Bend-La Pine, a concern goes first to the school, then to the superintendent's office, then to the school board, which decides whether an action followed policy. *\[Karen Rush mtg, Oct 15\]*  
* **Land use decisions** can be appealed to the [Land Use Board of Appeals (LUBA)](https://www.oregon.gov/luba). One catch: an issue usually must be raised at a local hearing, or it can't be raised on appeal. This applies only for quasi-judicial and legislative land use decisions; most land use decisions involving data center or infrastructure development would fall into these categories.   
* **Public meeting violations.** Anyone can file a written grievance with the public body within 30 days; the body has 21 days to respond. If it doesn't fix the problem, the person can complain to the [Oregon Government Ethics Commission](https://www.oregon.gov/ogec/Pages/default.aspx). Courts can also void decisions made in an unlawful meeting.   
* **Pushing for proper process.** Oregon Housing and Community Services emailed a handbook change barring funded organizations from using AI, "effective immediately." NeighborImpact argued that enforceable guidance must go through rulemaking with public comment, and the change is now on hold. *\[CC Mtg 3, Oct 9\]*  
* **Ballot measures.** Oregon voters can refer laws and many local decisions to the ballot, or propose their own through an initiative. 

* **Lawsuits.** Individuals and advocacy groups can bring legal action in court to challenge decisions, enforce public records laws, or block government actions that violate statutory or constitutional rights.
